---
title: "Policy Gradients"
---

The [previous chapter](01-what-makes-a-problem-rl.qmd) trained one policy three ways and ended
each step with the same operation: a gradient step on $\sum_i w_i\log\pi_\theta(y_i\mid x_i)$
over a batch of responses. That was not a coincidence of implementation. This chapter derives
the policy gradient from scratch and shows that it *is* that operation. Maximizing expected
reward produces a gradient that looks exactly like maximum-likelihood training, except that the
responses are ones the model sampled itself and each one carries a weight that can be negative.
This is the book's second thesis and the single most useful identity in it: almost every
post-training method, from SFT to PPO to DPO, can be written as a choice of **which responses**
and **what weight on each**. The second half of the chapter deals with the price of sampling:
the gradient estimate is noisy, and baselines, advantages and critics are the classical tools
for living with that noise.

## The problem

A policy $\pi_\theta(y\mid x)$ produces a response $y$ to a prompt $x$, and a reward function
$r(x,y)$ scores it. The goal is to maximize the expected reward,

$$
J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_x}\,\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}\big[r(x,y)\big].
$$

Two features make this different from minimizing a supervised loss. First, the reward is a black
box: it may be a rule-based checker, a human judgment or another network, and it need not be
differentiable in $y$. Even if it were, $y$ is a sequence of discrete tokens, so there is no
gradient to pass through it. Second, $\theta$ enters $J$ only through the *distribution* the
expectation is taken over. Changing $\theta$ does not change any response; it changes which
responses are likely. The question is how to differentiate an expectation with respect to the
parameters of the distribution it is taken over, using only samples and reward evaluations.

## Assumptions

1. **The policy is differentiable and has full support where it matters.** $\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y\mid x)$
   exists, and $\pi_\theta(y\mid x) > 0$ for responses we want gradients for. A softmax over the
   next token guarantees both. If the policy assigned exactly zero probability to good responses
   it could never sample them, and the gradient would never point toward them.
2. **We can sample from the current policy and evaluate the reward on the samples.** Nothing is
   assumed about the reward's form.
3. **Expectations and gradients can be exchanged.** True for the finite response spaces of
   language models (sums, not integrals).

## Derivation

### The one-step (bandit) case

Fix a prompt $x$ and drop it from the notation. Write the expectation as a sum and differentiate:

$$
\nabla_\theta J = \nabla_\theta\sum_y \pi_\theta(y)\,r(y) = \sum_y r(y)\,\nabla_\theta\pi_\theta(y).
$$

This is not yet usable, because $\sum_y r(y)\nabla_\theta\pi_\theta(y)$ is not an expectation
under anything we can sample from. The **log-derivative trick** makes it one. Since
$\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y) = \nabla_\theta\pi_\theta(y)/\pi_\theta(y)$, multiply and divide by
$\pi_\theta(y)$:

$$
\nabla_\theta J = \sum_y \pi_\theta(y)\,r(y)\,\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y)
= \mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_\theta}\big[\,r(y)\,\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y)\,\big].
$$

Now the gradient is an expectation under the policy itself. Sample $y_1,\dots,y_n$ from
$\pi_\theta$, evaluate their rewards, and average $r(y_i)\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_i)$. The
average is an unbiased estimate of $\nabla_\theta J$. The reward is never differentiated; it only
multiplies. This estimator is Williams's REINFORCE [@williams1992simple], also called the
*score-function* estimator, since $\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta$ is the score of the policy.

### The sequential case

A language model generates $y = (y_1,\dots,y_T)$ one token at a time, so by the chain rule
$\pi_\theta(y\mid x) = \prod_t\pi_\theta(y_t\mid s_t)$, where $s_t = (x, y_{<t})$ is the state
before token $t$. The log turns the product into a sum,

$$
\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y\mid x) = \sum_{t=1}^{T}\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_t\mid s_t),
$$

and nothing else in the derivation changes. Two things are worth noticing. The transition from
$s_t$ to $s_{t+1}$ never appears, because in general the environment's transition probabilities
do not depend on $\theta$ and drop out of $\nabla_\theta\log$ of the trajectory's probability; for
text generation the transition is deterministic anyway ("append the token"). And with one reward
at the end, every token's score is multiplied by the same scalar $r(x,y)$. In MDPs with rewards
along the way, the reward-to-go $G_t$ replaces $r$ at step $t$, because an action cannot affect
rewards that came before it. That is the general policy gradient theorem, in the Monte Carlo (REINFORCE) form derived by
Sutton and Barto [@sutton2018reinforcement, secs. 13.2–13.3]:

$$
\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta}\Big[\sum_t G_t\,\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)\Big].
$$

### The climax: put the SFT gradient next to it

Supervised fine-tuning maximizes the log-likelihood of demonstrations $(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}$. Its
gradient is

$$
\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}} = \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}\big[\,1\cdot\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y\mid x)\,\big],
$$

and the policy gradient is

$$
\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_x,\;y\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}\big[\,r(x,y)\cdot\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y\mid x)\,\big].
$$

**These are the same operation.** Each pushes up the log-probability of some sequences. They
differ in exactly two places: *which* sequences are used (a fixed dataset vs. the model's own
samples) and *how much weight* each one gets (always 1 vs. a reward that, after the baselines of
the next section, can be negative and push a sequence *down*).

@fig-sft-vs-reinforce-gradient shows this on the toy language, for a prompt that
$\pi_{\text{ref}}$ answers correctly 19% of the time. On the left are actual batches: SFT sees 16
demonstrations, all correct and all weighted $+1$; REINFORCE sees 16 of the policy's own samples,
and the correct ones get positive weight while the wrong ones get negative weight. On the right is
the *expected* coefficient that each method puts on each response's $\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y)$,
computed exactly for all 625 responses. SFT puts weight only on correct answers, in proportion to
the expert's probability for them, wherever they sit in the policy's ranking. REINFORCE puts
positive weight on correct answers in proportion to how likely *the policy* already finds them,
and an equal total of negative weight on the wrong answers it currently favors. The most likely
response under $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is wrong, so it receives the largest push down.

![Left: one batch per method for one prompt, with the weight on each response (responses ranked by $\pi_{\text{ref}}$; red = wrong answer). SFT trains on someone else's correct answers with weight $+1$; REINFORCE trains on its own samples with a signed weight (here the reward minus the mean of the other samples). Right: the exact expected coefficient $q(y)\,w(y)$ on $\nabla\log\pi(y)$ for all 625 responses. SFT's coefficient is the expert's distribution over correct answers. REINFORCE's is $\pi(y)\,(r(y)-\mathbb{E}[r])$: up on correct answers the policy already likes, down on wrong answers it likes, nothing on responses it never produces.](../images/sft_vs_reinforce_gradient.png){#fig-sft-vs-reinforce-gradient}

### The $(q, w)$ form

The comparison generalizes into the frame for the rest of the book.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition — The $(q,w)$ form of a post-training gradient"}
$$
\nabla_\theta\mathcal{J} \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_x,\;y\sim q(\cdot\mid x)}\Big[\,w(x,y)\,\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y\mid x)\,\Big] \;+\; \text{(regularizer gradient)}
$$
A method is specified by its **sampling distribution** $q$ (where the trained-on responses come
from) and its **per-sample weight** $w$ (or per-token weight $w_t$ on $\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y_t\mid s_t)$).
SFT: $q = $ the data, $w = 1$. REINFORCE: $q = \pi_\theta$, $w = r$ (or an advantage).
:::

This is not this book's invention. Shao et al. make the same observation in the DeepSeekMath
paper, writing the gradient of every method they study as an expectation over a **data source**
of a **gradient coefficient** times $\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta$, with the coefficient determined
by a **reward function** and an algorithm, and they tabulate SFT, rejection-sampling fine-tuning,
DPO, PPO and GRPO in those terms [@shao2024deepseekmath, sec. 5.2]. In the toy implementation
the form is literal: every method in `rl4llm.methods` ends in the same call,
`grad_log_likelihood(lang, logits, prompts, responses, weights)`, and differs only in the
`responses` it passes and the `weights` it computes.

::: {.callout-tip title="Method card — REINFORCE"}
| | |
|---|---|
| **Signal** | scalar reward per response |
| **Samples from** ($q$) | $\pi_\theta$, fresh samples every update (on-policy) |
| **Per-sample weight** ($w$) | the reward $r(x,y)$, or $r - b$ with a baseline |
| **Stability** | none beyond a small learning rate |
| **Credit granularity** | sequence level: the same weight on every token's score (reward-to-go $G_t$ per step in general MDPs) |
| **Models in memory** | policy (+ reward function) |
| **Targets** | $\max_\theta\mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta}[r]$, an unregularized objective |
| **Classical lineage** | Williams (1992); the Monte Carlo policy gradient (Sutton & Barto §13.3) |
:::

## Interpretation

What does following this gradient produce? It maximizes expected reward and nothing else. The
weight on each response is its reward, so mass flows toward whatever the reward function scores
highest. Nothing in the objective asks the policy to stay diverse or to stay close to where it
started. The [previous chapter](01-what-makes-a-problem-rl.qmd) showed the consequence: with a
0/1 correctness reward, REINFORCE ended with essentially all its probability on one correct
answer, where SFT on the same task kept the expert's spread. The KL penalty that every LLM recipe
adds, and the closed-form optimum it produces, are the subject of the
[chapter on keeping updates stable](03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd) and the
[shared-target chapter](06-the-shared-target.qmd). Before that, there is a more immediate problem.

## Variance, baselines and advantages

The estimator is unbiased, but a single sample tells you very little. Every response's score is
scaled by its reward, so the estimate depends on the reward's *level*, not just on which responses
are better. If all rewards are shifted up by 10, every sampled response gets pushed up hard; the
gradient is still right on average, because the pushes on likely responses cancel in expectation,
but each individual estimate is dominated by noise.

### Why subtracting a baseline does not bias the gradient

The score function has mean zero:

$$
\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_\theta}\big[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y)\big] = \sum_y\nabla_\theta\pi_\theta(y) = \nabla_\theta\sum_y\pi_\theta(y) = \nabla_\theta 1 = 0.
$$

So for any $b$ that does not depend on the sampled response,
$\mathbb{E}[(r(y)-b)\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y)] = \mathbb{E}[r(y)\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(y)]$.
Subtracting a **baseline** changes nothing in expectation and can change the variance a great
deal. Sutton and Barto note that the baseline "can be any function, even a random variable, as
long as it does not vary with" the action [@sutton2018reinforcement, sec. 13.4]. That condition
is the whole design space of baselines, and it explains each common choice.

- **A constant or running mean.** Unbiased. Removes the reward's overall level.
- **A per-prompt value $V(x) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta}[r\mid x]$.** Unbiased. In a prompt where
  every answer scores well, only answers *better than usual* get pushed up.
- **A learned critic $V_\phi(s_t)$, per token.** Unbiased as long as it depends only on the
  state, not on the token chosen there. This is the actor–critic architecture, and
  $r - V_\phi(s_t)$ is an estimate of the **advantage** $A(s_t,y_t)$ from the
  [previous chapter](01-what-makes-a-problem-rl.qmd).
- **Leave-one-out (RLOO).** Sample $G$ responses for the same prompt and use, for response $i$,
  the mean reward of the *other* $G-1$: $b_i = \frac{1}{G-1}\sum_{j\ne i}r_j$. Because $b_i$ is
  built from samples independent of $y_i$, it is unbiased, and it costs nothing beyond the extra
  samples. Kool, van Hoof and Welling proposed it under the memorable title "Buy 4 REINFORCE
  samples, get a baseline for free!" [@kool2019buy], and Ahmadian et al. brought it to RLHF
  [@ahmadian2024back].
- **The group mean including the sample itself.** Biased: $r_i$ appears in its own baseline with
  weight $1/G$, so the expected gradient is shrunk by $(G-1)/G$. Rescaling by $G/(G-1)$ turns it
  exactly into RLOO.
- **The group mean and standard deviation (GRPO).** Divides each prompt's centered rewards by that
  prompt's reward standard deviation. This is no longer only a baseline: it rescales different
  prompts differently and so changes *which objective* is being followed.
  [Policy Gradients Without a Critic](08-policy-gradients-without-a-critic.qmd) takes it apart.

::: {.callout-important title="Classical lineage — this is a Monte Carlo baseline"}
The baseline was already in Williams's original work [@sutton2018reinforcement, sec. 13.4
notes]. RLOO and GRPO's group mean are Monte Carlo baselines: estimates of $V(x)$ built from
extra samples instead of a learned network. A learned $V_\phi(s_t)$ is the critic of
actor–critic methods.
:::

### How much does a baseline actually help? A measurement

Textbook accounts often say that a baseline "reduces variance", full stop. The toy language can
check that claim, because the exact gradient is known. @fig-gradient-variance-by-baseline
compares thousands of stochastic gradient estimates with it.

![Relative mean squared error $\mathbb{E}\|\hat g - g\|^2/\|g\|^2$ of policy-gradient estimates against the exact gradient of $\mathbb{E}[r]$ (1,500 estimates per point). Left: at $\pi_{\text{ref}}$, with the reward shifted by a constant $c$; without a baseline the error grows with the square of the offset, while every baselined estimator is unaffected. Middle: at a good policy (85% correct), against the number of samples per prompt. Right: GAE's $\lambda$ with a critic that is close to, but not exactly, $V^\pi$; lowering $\lambda$ cuts variance and adds bias.](../images/gradient_variance_by_baseline.png){#fig-gradient-variance-by-baseline}

The left panel holds the policy at $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ and adds a constant $c$ to every reward. The
expected gradient is identical for every $c$. Without a baseline, the estimator's error is about
1.2 times $\|g\|^2$ at $c=0$ and about 80 times at $c=3$, growing with the square of the offset.
Every baselined estimator is flat. This is the most important thing a baseline buys, and it
matters more in LLM training than in the textbook setting: a reward model trained on preferences
is identifiable only up to a per-prompt constant ([the rewards chapter](05-rewards.qmd)), so its
offset is arbitrary. A baseline makes the gradient indifferent to it.

The same panel holds a surprise. At $c = 0$, the estimator *without* a baseline has the lowest
error of all. With a 0/1 reward and a policy that is usually wrong, most samples have reward 0 and
contribute nothing; zero happens to be close to the average reward, so it is already a decent
baseline. A baseline estimated from a few other samples adds its own noise, and here that costs
more than it saves. Once the policy is good (middle panel, 85% correct), the situation reverses:
most rewards are now 1, zero is a poor baseline, and every baselined estimator beats plain
REINFORCE at every group size. RLOO pays for estimating its baseline from only $G-1$ samples at
very small $G$ and has nearly caught up with the exact per-prompt value $V(x)$ by $G = 16$. The exact
per-token critic $V^\pi(s_t)$, the best a learned critic could be, is the best estimator at the
good policy, but only slightly. In this task every prefix can still be completed correctly by the
last token, so knowing the prefix says little about the outcome, and a per-token critic has
little to add over a per-prompt baseline. The general lesson is that **a baseline guarantees an
unchanged expectation and invariance to the reward's offset; how much it reduces variance depends
on the reward and the policy, and should be measured rather than assumed.**

### Generalized advantage estimation

A critic opens a second design dimension. With a learned $V_\phi$, the advantage of the token
chosen at $s_t$ can be estimated by the full Monte Carlo return minus the baseline,
$G_t - V_\phi(s_t)$, or by the one-step **temporal-difference error**
$\delta_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma V_\phi(s_{t+1}) - V_\phi(s_t)$, which bootstraps from the critic's
estimate of the next state. Schulman et al.'s **generalized advantage estimator** (GAE)
interpolates with an exponentially weighted sum of TD errors [@schulman2015gae]:

::: {.callout-note title="Definition — Generalized advantage estimation"}
$$
\hat A_t^{\text{GAE}(\gamma,\lambda)} = \sum_{l=0}^{\infty}(\gamma\lambda)^l\,\delta_{t+l},
\qquad \delta_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma V_\phi(s_{t+1}) - V_\phi(s_t).
$$
$\lambda = 1$ gives $G_t - V_\phi(s_t)$; $\lambda = 0$ gives $\delta_t$.
:::

The paper states the trade-off precisely. $\lambda = 1$ is unbiased "regardless of the accuracy
of $V$, but it has high variance due to the sum of terms"; $\lambda = 0$ is unbiased only if the
critic is exact "and otherwise induces bias, but it typically has much lower variance"
[@schulman2015gae, sec. 3]. The right panel of @fig-gradient-variance-by-baseline measures it with
a critic that equals the true value plus a fixed error of standard deviation 0.15 per state.
Moving $\lambda$ from 1 to 0 cuts the variance from about 2.5 to 1.6 (relative to $\|g\|^2$) and
raises the squared bias from about 0.001 to 0.1; the total error is lowest at intermediate
$\lambda$. This is the bias–variance trade-off of bootstrapping from the
[previous chapter](01-what-makes-a-problem-rl.qmd), now inside a policy-gradient estimator. GAE
is what PPO-based RLHF uses ([the shared-target chapter](06-the-shared-target.qmd)), and its
dependence on a good critic is one reason later LLM recipes dropped the critic altogether.

::: {.callout-important title="Classical lineage — this is TD(λ), applied to advantages"}
GAE is built exactly like the λ-return of TD(λ), as its authors note, "however TD(λ) is an
estimator of the value function, whereas here we are estimating the advantage function"
[@schulman2015gae]. The λ dial is the Monte Carlo vs. TD dial from every RL course.
:::

## Behavior and failure modes

**No variation, no signal.** With a baseline built from the same group, a prompt where every
sampled response gets the same reward produces advantages of exactly zero, whether all the
answers were right or all wrong. On the hard prompt of the
[previous chapter](01-what-makes-a-problem-rl.qmd), most early groups were all wrong, and learning
stalled until the policy happened onto correct answers.
[Policy Gradients Without a Critic](08-policy-gradients-without-a-critic.qmd) quantifies how often
this happens and what DAPO's dynamic sampling does about it.

**On-policy, strictly.** The derivation required $y\sim\pi_\theta$ for the *current* $\theta$.
The moment the policy is updated, last step's samples come from the wrong distribution, and
reusing them gives a biased gradient. Every practical method reuses samples somewhat, for
efficiency, and needs a correction (importance ratios) and a guard against using it too far (a
trust region). That is the [next chapter](03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd).

**The objective has no brakes.** As noted under Interpretation, $\mathbb{E}[r]$ rewards collapse
onto whatever scores highest, and with a learned reward, onto whatever *fools the reward model*
([the rewards chapter](05-rewards.qmd)).

**Credit is smeared across tokens.** A single sequence-level weight multiplies every token's
score, so the tokens that mattered and the tokens that did not are pushed equally. On average
the irrelevant pushes cancel; on any one sample they are noise. Per-token critics, process
rewards and dense teacher signals
([Learning by Imitating a Better Distribution](09-imitating-a-better-distribution.qmd)) are all
attempts to fix this.
